deep.reconstruction:
The page has five separate entries, divided by horizontal rules.

(0) Heading: a single word, read by the machine as 'Reithandelt.' The reading is uncertain and its meaning is unclear. It has no mathematical content.

(1) Methodological maxim (no mathematics). A formula or calculation is justified either as an example or as a tool (e.g. in the theory of power series). It is never the mark of progress or an end in itself. Just as the real goal must not be lost over refining the means, the guiding and driving idea must not be forgotten over formula manipulation. This continues the previous page ('the problem comes first; the method serves it, it is not an end in itself').

(2) Bibliographic note. A complete list of the literature on primes is kept in Hilbert's own notes 'Versuche, betreffend die Theorie der Primzahlen'.

(3) An Abelian route to the divergence of sum 1/p.
- Hilbert's claim: by means of a power series sum l_n x^n, one can compute lim_{eps->0} sum_p 1/(p(1+eps p)), i.e. say how fast it tends to infinity.
- The series is transcribed 'Sum ln x^n'. Most plausibly l_n = 1/n for n prime and 0 otherwise, so the series is sum_p x^p/p.
- My reconstruction of the link (not on the page):
  - 1/(1+eps p) = int_0^oo e^{-u(1+eps p)} du.
  - Hence S(eps) := sum_p 1/(p(1+eps p)) = int_0^oo e^{-u} P(e^{-eps u}) du, where P(x) = sum_p x^p/p.
  - So the growth of S(eps) as eps->0 follows from the growth of P(x) as x->1-.
- Expected answer (mine, via Mertens): S(eps) is essentially sum_{p<1/eps} 1/p, which is about log log(1/eps) + const.

(4) Research plan: work through Dirichlet's proof of infinitely many primes in arithmetic progressions.
- Question 1: is the proof that L_{+1} and L_{-1} are nonzero perhaps unnecessary? Here L_{+1}, L_{-1} are evidently Dirichlet's series for the (real) characters; compare '≠ +1, ≠ -1, ≠ 0' on the next page.
- Proposed substitute: use the theorem on the cyclotomic equation. The left side Phi_p(x) = (x^p-1)/(x-1) has, at integer arguments, only prime divisors of the form kp+1 (apart from p itself).
- With that, compute directly the asymptotics of sum_{q<N, q prime, q ≡ 1 mod p} 1/q, as Chebyshev and Mertens did for sum_{q<N} 1/q over all primes.
- Mertens (1874): sum_{q<=N} 1/q = log log N + M + O(1/log N).
- The upper limit is written 'p<N'; it should be q<N.
- The plan is continued on the next page (Stirling series for complex arguments after Stieltjes; avoiding definite integrals).
- Implicit content, supplied by me:
  - Taking logarithms of prod_{n<=x} Phi_p(n) gives roughly (p-1) x log x.
  - All prime factors are ≡ 1 mod p or equal to p.
  - A Chebyshev-type bookkeeping then yields sum_{q≡1(p), q<=x} log q/q >> log x, hence divergence of sum 1/q over that class.
  - This handles only the residue class 1 mod p.
errors: Entry (4): the cyclotomic argument controls only primes ≡ 1 (mod p). It cannot replace the nonvanishing of L(1,chi) for general residue classes a mod p. Moreover, elementary methods of Chebyshev type give lower bounds (divergence) easily, but an exact Mertens-type asymptotic (1/(p-1)) log log N for the class 1 mod p still requires L(1,chi) ≠ 0 or equivalent information. Hilbert's question 1 therefore has a negative answer as stated, though a partial (one-class) version works.
Entry (4): the summation bound is written p<N while the summation variable is q (prime, q = kp+1). It should be q<N. The 'p' in the denominator '1/(pq)' is a struck-through remnant.

Entry (3): the statement is only a claim, with no derivation on the page. The required Tauberian/Abelian passage from P(x) = sum x^p/p near x=1 to S(eps) needs knowledge of P(x) ~ log log(1/(1-x)), which itself is essentially Mertens's theorem. So the method is somewhat circular unless P is controlled independently (e.g. via log zeta).

results.what: Formulas are tools or examples, never the goal; the leading idea must not be lost in calculation
results.modern_name: Hilbert's methodological maxim (cf. 'Gedanken statt Rechnungen', Zahlbericht preface 1897)
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (attitude well known; echoes Dirichlet/Riemann tradition)

results.what: Growth of sum_p 1/(p(1+eps p)) as eps->0 via the power series sum_p x^p/p
results.modern_name: Abelian summation / smoothed Mertens theorem: sum_p 1/(p(1+eps p)) ~ log log(1/eps)
results.usually_credited_to: Mertens 1874 (sum 1/p); Abelian methods: Euler, Dirichlet, Chebyshev

results.what: Replace the L(1,chi) ≠ 0 step in Dirichlet's theorem by the fact that prime divisors of Phi_p(n) are ≡ 1 mod p, and estimate sum 1/q over q ≡ 1 mod p à la Chebyshev–Mertens
results.modern_name: Elementary (cyclotomic) proof of Dirichlet's theorem for the class 1 mod m, with quantitative divergence
results.usually_credited_to: Qualitative infinitude: Lebesgue 1859, Sylvester 1888, Wendt 1895; quantitative elementary versions later (e.g. Nagell, Rosser-type arguments); the general case needs L(1,chi) ≠ 0 (Dirichlet 1837, elementary: Mertens 1895-97, Selberg 1949)

deep.surprise_reason: These are research-plan notes, not results. The cyclotomic route to primes ≡ 1 mod p was known (Lebesgue, Sylvester), and the smoothing of sum 1/p is standard. Hilbert's interest in simplifying Dirichlet's proof is a modest biographical detail, of minor interest for dating his early number-theory studies.

transcription_corrections: 'Σ ln x^n' is more likely 'Σ l_n x^n' (a power series with coefficients l_n), not a sum of logarithms.
'Σ^{p<N} 1/(pq)': the 'p' in the denominator is struck through. The intended expression is Σ^{p<N} 1/q with q = kp+1 (the bound should logically be q<N).
Heading 'Reithandelt.' is uncertain; the first letters could also be read differently. It is not a mathematical term.
